opus-5.5.text:
I think the gap is actually much bigger than most people feel when they watch those videos.

When you see a robot doing kung fu flips or dancing on stage, that's genuinely impressive engineering. The hardware has improved a lot, the motor control is better, and reinforcement learning in simulation with sim-to-real transfer has gotten good. But those performances are mostly rehearsed. The environment is controlled, the motion is choreographed, and the robot doesn't need to understand anything about the world around it. In some sense it's closer to a very sophisticated playback than to intelligence.

Caring for someone at home is a completely different problem. Your home is messy. Every home is different. Objects are deformable, lighting changes, people move unpredictably, and the tasks are long-horizon and open-ended. You have to understand that the cup is fragile, that the elderly person might fall, that this drawer sticks a little. That requires perception, common sense about physics, memory, planning, and the ability to recover from mistakes. And above all, safety. A backflip that fails 5% of the time is fine for a demo. A robot that drops someone 5% of the time is unacceptable.

So I'd say the "body" part is progressing fast, but the "brain" part, real spatial understanding and a grounded model of the world, is still very early. This is also why I care so much about visual intelligence and world models. Language models learned from the internet, but there's no internet-scale dataset of embodied experience, and text alone doesn't teach you how the physical world works. Until we have systems that can genuinely perceive, predict, and reason about 3D space and physical interaction, general-purpose home robots will stay mostly a vision.

I don't want to be too pessimistic. I think we'll see useful robots in narrower, structured settings first, like factories and warehouses, and that's valuable. But the step from a spectacular demo to something you'd trust with your grandparents is not incremental. It probably needs some fundamental breakthroughs, not just more scaling of what we have now.

r001.rationale: The response says the robot’s “brain” is still very early and describes the missing perception, common sense, memory, planning, and physical-world reasoning needed for home care, identifying intelligence as the main gap.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the gap is enormous, and it's a gap of kind, not of degree.

When you see a humanoid doing a backflip or a martial arts routine, what you're really watching is a control problem that has been solved very well. The environment is known, the sequence is fixed, and you can rehearse it thousands of times in simulation before the robot ever moves. It's genuinely impressive engineering, especially the hardware and the low-level control, but it's closer to a very good animation playing back on a physical body than to intelligence.

Caring for someone at home is almost the opposite setting. Nothing is fixed. The lighting changes, the cup is in a different place, the person moves unexpectedly, there's a cat on the floor. The robot has to perceive a messy, open-ended world, understand what matters in it, and then act with fine manipulation, often while physically touching a human being, where a mistake isn't a fall on a stage but an actual injury. That demands perception, world understanding, long-horizon reasoning, and dexterous manipulation all working together, with very high reliability. We don't have any one of those at the needed level, let alone all of them together.

From my side, as someone who works mostly on vision and representation learning, I'd say the real bottleneck is not the body. The bodies are getting pretty good. The bottleneck is the brain, and specifically the visual and physical understanding. Our current vision-language models still have surprisingly shallow spatial reasoning. They can describe a scene, but ask them which object is in front, how far something is, whether a grasp will work, and they're often wrong. A caregiving robot needs that kind of understanding to be nearly flawless.

The other piece is data. Language models got their capabilities from essentially the entire internet. Robots have nothing comparable. Teleoperation data is expensive and small, simulation has a reality gap, and video from the internet doesn't come with actions attached. So a lot of the interesting research now is about whether we can learn useful world models and representations from passive video, so the robot doesn't have to learn everything through its own slow, costly experience.

So my honest assessment is that demos make it look like we're one step away, and we're not. I'm optimistic over a decade or so, especially as vision foundation models get grounded in physics and 3D. But I'd be cautious about anyone implying that a robot that can do kung fu today can help your grandmother tomorrow. Those are different problems, and the second one is much harder.

r001.rationale: The response says the main bottleneck is the robot’s “brain,” specifically its visual and physical understanding, and describes current capabilities as insufficient for household care.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s still a substantial gap. A robot performing martial arts can demonstrate impressive control and balance, but that alone doesn’t tell us how well it can handle unfamiliar situations. The key question is how much of the performance depends on a rehearsed sequence and a carefully controlled environment.

A home is much less predictable. If you ask a robot to help someone drink water, it needs to find the right cup, handle it safely, understand whether the person needs assistance, and respond if something goes wrong. Each individual action might look less impressive than a backflip, but putting them together reliably is a much broader problem.

And caring for people raises the bar further. The robot needs to recognize uncertainty and know when to stop or ask for help. A demonstration can tolerate occasional failures; a robot helping an elderly person can’t treat safety as an average success rate.

So I see these performances as meaningful progress in physical capabilities. But general-purpose home assistance also requires perception, reasoning, learning, and reliable interaction with people. We shouldn’t assume that solving the impressive-looking movements means we’ve solved those other pieces.

r001.rationale: The response describes a broad gap involving perception, reasoning, learning, and reliability, but it does not identify insufficient robotic intelligence as the main bottleneck.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the gap is still very large. A robot doing martial arts or performing onstage can be impressive, but you have to ask what that demonstration actually tells us. How much was rehearsed? How controlled is the environment? What happens if something unexpected occurs?

Taking care of someone at home is a very different problem. Every home is different, objects move around, and people don’t always express what they need clearly. The robot has to perceive the situation, understand the person’s intention, manipulate objects, and recover when it makes a mistake. And it has to do all of that safely, over long periods of time.

So I would distinguish the ability to execute a difficult movement from the ability to handle an unfamiliar situation. The first is real progress, but it doesn’t automatically give you the second. For home care, reliability matters much more than how impressive a single demonstration looks. The question is whether the robot can consistently do useful things—and recognize when it should stop and ask for help.

r001.rationale: The response describes challenges such as perceiving situations, understanding intentions, and handling unfamiliar events, but it does not identify insufficient robotic intelligence as the main bottleneck.
